key: He who vanquishes yet still Keeps from his foes apart; He whose hests men most fulfil Yet humbly plies his art.
s: In a chapter on the skilled warrior, the verse turns to victory and command; the Heshang Gong commentary, on chapter 68, reads the victor as winning by benevolence and virtue, so foes yield without contest, and the good user of men as keeping below them.
src: The Heshang Gong commentary, Laozi Daodejing Heshang Gong zhangju, chapter 68, zh.wikisource (a normalised text), revision 1552800 (2019)

opened.locator: chapter 68 (配天), comments on 善勝敵者不與 and 善用人者為之下
opened.edition: zh.wikisource 老子河上公章句, revision 1552800 (a normalised text)

evidence.words: 善以道勝敵者，附近以仁，來遠以德，不與敵爭，而敵自服也。…善用人自輔佐者，常為人執謙下也。
evidence.gloss: One good at conquering enemies by the Tao draws the near with benevolence and brings the distant with virtue; he does not contend with the enemy, and the enemy submits of itself. One good at using men to assist him always keeps himself humble and below them.
evidence.licence: public domain text; transcription CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource)

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, ref Tao Te Ching 68, at [67]); its two couplets are Legge’s rendering of 善勝敵者不與 and 善用人者為之下, the very lines the Heshang Gong commentary glosses. Its comment on the first: winning by the Tao, drawing the near by benevolence and the distant by virtue, not contending, so the enemy submits of itself; on the second: always keeping humble and below others. The sentence’s paraphrase stays within these words. Plain sense (a chapter on the skilled warrior, the verse turning to victory and command) is faithful with Legge’s parenthesis struck out. entry-check ok, 45 words.
